notes: Loss Relief GLO procedural jurisdiction appeal; Hoechst principle and group loss relief statutory route are clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Group loss relief claims and statutory tax appeal procedure after Hoechst
key_facts: Following the ECJ decision in Hoechst, 59 test claimants in the Loss Relief GLO sought restitution and damages from the Inland Revenue over UK group loss relief rules.
The Revenue applied to strike out category (i) claims for group loss relief, arguing they should follow the statutory route of claim to the Inspector and appeal to the Commissioners.
Park J struck out the group loss relief paragraphs and refused permission to appeal.
Six test claimants were at different stages of making statutory claims to Inspectors of Taxes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted from a strike-out application in Chancery group litigation on whether High Court proceedings for group loss relief were permissible.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judge's order discharged and Revenue's strike-out application dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Consistently with Hoechst, where UK tax law denied mixed-resident groups the benefit of group loss relief, it is contrary to Community law for the High Court to refuse category (i) claims solely because the statutory tax appeal procedure was not followed; the principle of effectiveness requires the High Court to entertain such claims.
legal_issues: Whether group loss relief claims must be brought via the statutory Inspector and Commissioners procedure
Effect of the ECJ decision in Hoechst on national procedural rules
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction or should exercise discretion to decline jurisdiction
Whether failure to use the statutory procedure was a bar to restitution claims based on Community law

notes: Argentine railway reinsurance service-out application; serious issues and forum conveniens analysis are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Argentine reinsurance pessification dispute: service out upheld

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations 1980

key_facts: Tryg, a London reinsurer, obtained permission to serve declaratory proceedings on four Argentine fronting insurers over railway liability reinsurances.
The Defendants applied to set aside service, arguing no serious issue, inappropriate forum, and material non-disclosure.
Claims concerned pessification of US dollar reinsurance limits under Argentine decrees, late notification, follow-the-settlements, and legal costs coverage.
Schedule 2 listed 2,530 notified losses; the reinsurance book was said to represent about $60m in run-off.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside or stay permission to serve proceedings out of the jurisdiction on foreign reinsurers.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to serve out upheld for declarations 1, 2 and 4; proceedings on declaration 3 stayed; Tryg awarded a substantial proportion of costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where London-market reinsurance contracts are governed by English law and raise construction issues on conditions precedent and pessification, England is the appropriate forum; Tryg had realistic prospects on the serious-issue test for the main declarations, and alleged non-disclosure on notification arrangements was not material.
legal_issues: Whether CPR Part 6.20 gateway requirements were satisfied
Whether negative declarations had serious issues and practical utility
Whether Argentina or England was the forum conveniens
Whether permission to serve should be set aside for material non-disclosure

notes: School permanent exclusion JR; IAP decision and DfES guidance application are straightforward on the facts found.

enrichment.short_title: Permanent school exclusion for knife possession upheld on appeal

statutes_considered.title: Education (Pupil Exclusions and Appeals) (Maintained Schools) (England) Regulations 2002

key_facts: M, a pupil with special educational needs at Nightingale School, was found in possession of a knife on school premises in October 2003.
The head teacher initially viewed the incident as minor but, after reviewing CCTV and witness reports, recommended permanent exclusion.
The governing body and independent appeal panel upheld permanent exclusion under the school's behaviour policy.
M argued the IAP applied the policy mechanically without assessing whether permanent exclusion was a reasonable response.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of decisions by the school governing body and independent appeal panel upholding permanent exclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; challenge to the IAP decision failed; permission to appeal refused; claimant ordered to pay defendants' costs subject to LSC proviso.
enrichment.ratio: The IAP did not decide the appeal solely by reference to the behaviour policy; it considered M's account, DfES guidance, and made the critical finding that he was not intending to hand in the knife when first asked, which was a rational basis for upholding permanent exclusion for weapon possession.
legal_issues: Whether the IAP misdirected itself by applying school policy without regard to seriousness
Whether the IAP failed to make necessary findings of fact
Whether prior procedural unfairness before the governing body tainted the IAP decision
Admissibility of witness statements giving ex post facto justifications

notes: Bond trustee indemnity Wednesbury challenge; Elektrim acceleration risk analysis is thorough though confidential annex not visible.

enrichment.short_title: Bond trustee entitled to reject inadequate acceleration indemnity
key_facts: Concord, representing bondholders holding about 45% of €510m Elektrim bonds, sought a declaration that Law Debenture must accelerate the bonds.
Peter Smith J had held Elektrim's suspension of a bondholder-nominated director was a certifiable event of default materially prejudicial to bondholders.
Over 30% of bondholders requested acceleration, but the trustee required indemnity to its satisfaction before giving notice.
Concord offered indemnities from Elliott Associates LP which the trustee rejected as financially inadequate given potential €876m liability from wrongful acceleration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declaration that the bond trustee was obliged forthwith to accelerate bonds after event-of-default certification.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; trustee's conclusion that indemnities offered on 23 and 28 April 2004 were unsatisfactory was not Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: A trustee's contractual right to be indemnified to its satisfaction before accelerating bonds is for its own protection; on a worst-case scenario a wrongful acceleration could expose the trustee to a very large claim by Elektrim, and rejecting unsupported indemnities from Elliott Associates was not irrational in the Wednesbury sense.
legal_issues: Whether the trustee acted Wednesbury unreasonably in rejecting offered indemnities
Whether acceleration could give rise to a substantial damages claim by Elektrim
Whether trust deed exclusion and indemnity clauses protected the trustee
Whether the trustee could require secured indemnity rather than bare indemnity

notes: Military pension PAT appeal on bipolar attribution; procedural fairness point leading to remittal is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Military pension appeal remitted over bullying causation evidence
key_facts: Mr Carver enlisted aged 15 in 1962 and lost his left eye in a domestic incident while on leave in 1964, leading to invaliding out in 1965.
He later claimed a pension for bipolar affective disorder; the Secretary of State accepted the diagnosis but denied service attribution.
The Pensions Appeal Tribunal allowed the appeal on bipolar disorder, finding bullying in service together with the eye loss caused the condition.
Bullying had not been raised before the hearing and no expert medical evidence on causation had been obtained.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the Secretary of State with permission of the President of the Pensions Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; PAT decision on bipolar disorder set aside and matter remitted to a fresh tribunal for further hearing and directions.
enrichment.ratio: Where a wholly new causation case based on in-service bullying emerged at the PAT hearing without prior notice or expert evidence, fairness required an adjournment; the tribunal was not entitled to conclude service attribution on the sparse material before it.
legal_issues: Whether there was evidence supporting service attribution of bipolar affective disorder
Whether the PAT gave adequate reasons
Whether the Secretary of State was treated unfairly when bullying causation was raised for the first time at hearing

confidence.notes: Remittal reasoning and procedural unfairness finding are explicit. Substantive medical causation was deliberately left for the fresh tribunal.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition to Italy refused on habeas corpus challenges
key_facts: Italy sought Savvas's extradition on four cannabis conspiracy charges under the European Convention on Extradition.
District Judge Pratt committed him at Bow Street after a conjoined hearing with co-accused Casale and Guarneri.
Savvas applied for habeas corpus challenging identification, sufficiency of evidence on importation charge 1, and dual criminality on charge 3.
Identification rested on name, Hounslow birth and residence, and passport data extracted from co-accused papers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for habeas corpus following committal for extradition to Italy.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; all three grounds rejected; committal upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Identification to the criminal standard was established by name, date of birth and residence evidence and by authenticated passport information from conjoined proceedings; the import and possession charges were supported by the overarching conspiracy allegation; dual criminality was satisfied by comparing conduct with Italian Article 73 rather than requiring identical offence labels.
legal_issues: Whether identification was proved to the criminal standard
Whether a district judge could rely on material from a co-accused's extradition file
Whether evidence supported the importation conspiracy charge
Whether charge 3 satisfied dual criminality under section 2(1)(a)

notes: Planning LDC challenge on Use Classes intensification; Brookes and Burton application is authoritative and clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Lawful development certificate for Asda mezzanine retail intensification

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: Asda sought a lawful development certificate to install a mezzanine floor adding about 4,645 sq m of retail space at an Eastleigh store.
Eastleigh refused the certificate, arguing intensification of Class A1 shop use was a material change of use.
The store had grown from about 50,000 sq ft permitted in 1972 to about 83,000 sq ft without sales-area conditions.
The Secretary of State's inspector granted the certificate; the council challenged the decision by judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an inspector's decision granting a lawful development certificate under section 192.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; inspector's certificate upheld; permission to appeal refused; Secretary of State awarded agreed costs of £3,620.
enrichment.ratio: Under Brookes and Burton, intensification of use within the same Use Class does not constitute development enforceable under the Use Classes Order even if it might otherwise amount to a material change of use; a mezzanine increasing A1 retail space therefore could lawfully be certified.
legal_issues: Whether mezzanine retail expansion was development or a material change of use
Application of section 55(2)(f) and the 1987 Use Classes Order to intensification
Whether the inspector adequately considered planning effects under Wilson v West Sussex
Whether original permission square footage limits constrained lawful development

enrichment.short_title: HRA and article 8 in unfair dismissal of charity worker cautioned for gross indecency
key_facts: The applicant, a youth charity development officer, was cautioned for gross indecency with another man in a public transport café lavatory.
He did not disclose the caution to his employer, which worked with young offenders and the probation service.
He was summarily dismissed for gross misconduct after police checks triggered by probation funding revealed the caution.
He claimed unfair dismissal invoking article 8 and article 14 of the Convention via the Human Rights Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on Human Rights Act points in an unfair dismissal claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; employment tribunal correctly held dismissal fair and article 8 not engaged; reporting restrictions continued.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 HRA requires employment tribunals to interpret section 98 ERA compatibly with Convention rights in private employer cases, but article 8 was not engaged where conduct occurred in a public lavatory, amounted to a criminal offence and led to a caution relevant to employment; dismissal for non-disclosure and the offence was within the range of reasonable responses.
legal_issues: Horizontal effect of the Human Rights Act in unfair dismissal claims against private employers
Whether article 8 protected consensual sexual activity in a public lavatory
Whether section 98 ERA must be read compatibly with Convention rights under section 3
Whether dismissal based on a discriminatory Sexual Offences Act provision violated article 14

notes: Administration appointment timing and lease surrender injunction; paragraph 19 construction and estoppel points are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Injunction refused to block HDS lease surrender in Fliptex administration
key_facts: Fliptex, owner of Houston Business Centre, was put into administration on 24 November 2003 by debenture holders D3 and D4.
HDS Studios, Fliptex's tenant and subsidiary, sought to surrender two ten-year leases with £640,000 annual rent.
Mr Singh, Fliptex's director, sought to restrain acceptance of surrender to preserve a BBC studio licence and refinancing strategy.
Vacant possession was valued at about £7.8m, potentially enabling full payment of Fliptex's creditors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for injunction restraining administrators from accepting lease surrenders during Fliptex administration.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction application dismissed; administrators validly appointed on 24 November 2003; Fliptex estopped from challenging appointment by delay.
enrichment.ratio: An out-of-court administrator appointment under Schedule B1 takes effect only when paragraph 18 requirements are satisfied, so the appointment was effective on 24 November when documents were filed after demand; alternatively Fliptex was estopped from denying validity after acquiescing for months.
legal_issues: Whether administrators were validly appointed before debenture enforcement
Construction of Schedule B1 paragraph 19 effective date of appointment
Whether Fliptex was unable to pay its debts as they fell due
Balance of convenience for injunctive relief blocking lease surrender
linked_authorities: Byblos Bank v Al-Khudhary [1987] BCLC 232

notes: Share sale promissory note construction for Romanian MOH deal; summary judgment granted with forgery defence rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Summary judgment on deferred share price tied to Romanian sovereign guarantee
key_facts: Mr Dyer sold his 25% stake in Medrom SA to Piclux under a Share Sale Agreement dated 4 August 2001 for deferred payments under a promissory note.
Payments were conditional on issuance of Romanian Government sovereign guarantees for Medrom's Ministry of Health medical equipment contracts.
Mr von Habsburg guaranteed Piclux's obligations and lodged cheques as security, later disputed as corporate rather than personal.
Dyer claimed $1.115m balance; Defendants argued guarantees were not 'issued' until released from escrow to Medrom.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-applications for summary judgment on breach of Share Sale Agreement, promissory note and personal guarantee.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for Dyer against Piclux and von Habsburg for principal sum and contractual interest; sovereign guarantee held issued on delivery to escrow agent.
enrichment.ratio: In the commercial context of the MOH Deal, 'issue of the Sovereign Guarantee' meant when the Romanian Government signed and delivered guarantees to the escrow bank, triggering the contract and enabling Medrom to perform; Defendants' forgery and Luxembourg attachment defences had no real prospect of success.
legal_issues: Construction of 'issue of the Sovereign Guarantee' in the promissory note
Whether conditions precedent to deferred share payments were satisfied
Validity of the April 2002 Addendum and personal cheque security obligation
Effect of Luxembourg attachment orders on enforceability of the debt
linked_authorities: Baring v Commissioner of Inland Revenue [1898] 1 QB 78
Terrapin International Ltd v IRC [1976] 1 WLR 665

confidence.notes: Construction issue and summary judgment outcome are clearly reasoned. Luxembourg law was treated as equivalent to English law without dispute.
